Confirm diagnosis with chest radiographs; consider CT if additional characterization of lesion is needed or additional pathology is suspected. C

Intravenous ampicillin plus sulbactam or intravenous clindamycin are the recommended initial empiric antibiotic choice, with the addition of intravenous vancomycin or intravenous linezolid if community-acquired methicillin-resistant staphylococcus aureus (CA-MRSA) is suspected. Provide double coverage with antipseudomonal agents if healthcare-acquired pneumonia is suspected. B
The duration of antibiotic therapy is at least 3 weeks or until complete resolution of abscess. C
Consider surgical drainage in nonresponders, when malignancy is suspected or if hemorrhage is present. C
Overall mortality is approximately 10%, but higher in immunocompromised patients. B

background.definition: Pulmonary abscess is necrosis of lung tissue and formation of cavities by microbial infections.

list.listitem: Unknown in general population.
There is no accurate incidence of hospitalizations available. Aspiration pneumonias are estimated to be 5% to 10% of pneumonias requiring hospital admission.
Less than 1 in 100,000 per year of pediatric hospitalizations in Canada.
In a series of 5151 admitted with pneumonia, approximately 1% were complicated by lung abscess.
Oral pathogens are most common: Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus, and Prevotella; usually as mixed infection.
Staphylococcus: consider CA-MRSA.
Pseudomonas aeroginosa: especially if acquired in a hospital.
Rarely other organisms such as actinomyces, fungus, M. tuberculosis, and other atypical mycobacteria.
In the ICU, Enterobacteriaceae, Staphylococcus aureus, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa are the most commonon organisms and over one-third are nosocomial.
There is usually a predisposition to aspiration in patients with alcoholism, seizures, or stroke, and in those undergoing anesthesia or taking medications that could alter sensorium.
Poor lung clearance and defense mechanisms, with inflammation of lung tissue followed by necrosis.
A postobstructive abscess secondary to an endobronchial lesion may be seen in some cases.
Occasionally the spread is hematogenous, as in tricuspid valve endocarditis or septic phlebitis.

Improved oral hygiene can decrease the incidence in elderly patients who are aspiration prone. In a RCT, 407 nursing home patients were randomized to receive oral care or no oral care and were followed up for 2 years. A total of 11% in the oral care group and 19% in the control group developed pneumonia (NNT = 13). B
Suspect pulmonary abscess in patients with high risk of aspiration and who have signs and symptoms of RTI; onset is usually insidious. C

The initial imaging should be a CXR, which indicates abscess with air fluid level. Order chest CT when better characterization of abscess is needed or additional pathology, such as malignancy, empyema, or obstructive lesions, are suspected. C
Order sputum and blood cultures for aerobes and anaerobes. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Usually multiple lesions, other clinical and radiologic signs
Acid fast bacilli in sputum, nonresponse to medications

list.listitem: Symptoms are similar to those of patients with pneumonia. Patients typically present with fever, malaise, and cough.
Patients usually present with cough and copious amounts of purulent sputum.
Weight loss and pleuritic pain are common; purulent sputum is seen in approximately 50% of cases. Cavernous breath sounds and clubbing may be present.

A high index of suspicion is important: Consider lung abscess in patients who are not responding to initial antibiotic therapy, with risk factors for aspiration, such as stroke or drug use, those with healthcare-acquired pneumonia, and those who are immunocompromised.
CXR are the recommended initial study when abscess is suspected.
Chest CT is more accurate than CXR. Key characteristics include lung compression, wall characteristics, and pleural separation.

Chest CT is considered the gold standard for the diagnosis of lung abscess but is not necessary for all patients. Order chest CT when better characterization of abscess is needed or additional pathology like malignancy, empyema, or obstructive lesions are suspected.

Lung ultrasound is of limited value in the diagnosis of lung abscess; it may have a role in percutaneous drainage when CT-guided drainage is not possible. It may be an option as an initial test in children to avoid radiation exposure, but should be followed by CT if ultrasound is not definitive.
Order sputum culture, including anaerobic testing. Blood culture is rarely positive if only anaerobes are present.

Consider pulmonary abscess and order chest x-ray in patients with clinical features of pneumonia and who are are at high risk for aspiration. Consider chest CT to better characterize lung lesion or if additional pathology is suspected.
Initial empiric antibiotic should include anaerobic coverage; order sputum and blood cultures to guide subsequent therapy.

Consider bronchoscopy if there is no clinical improvement, suspicion of malignancy, or obstruction. Surgical drainage is rarely needed; consider surgery if failure to respond, obstruction, malignancy, or hemorrhage.
Intravenous ampicillin plus sulbactam or intravenous clindamycin are the recommended initial empiric antibiotic choice. B
Add intravenous vancomycin or linezolid if CA-MRSA is suspected and provide double coverage with antipseudomonal agents if healthcare-acquired pneumonia is suspected. C
Switch from intravenous to oral antibiotics when patient is hemodynamically stable, clinically improving, and able to take oral medications. B
The duration of antibiotic therapy is at least 3 weeks or until complete resolution of abscess. C
Consider surgical drainage in nonresponders, when malignancy is suspected, or if hemorrhage is present. C

Empiric antibiotic therapy should cover anaerobic bacteria. In an open-label RCT, 140 patients were randomized to receive either ampicillin 2 gm plus sulbactam 1 gm intravenously 3 times daily or clindamycin 600 mg intravenously 3 times daily with or without a second-generation or third-generation cephalosporin. All patients were given at least 6 days of intravenous therapy, followed by oral therapy for a mean of 23 to 24 days. Clinical response was 73% for ampicillin plus sulbactam and 67% for clindamycin with or without cephalosporin.
Add intravenous vancomycin or linezolid if CA-MRSA is suspected or identified.
Provide double coverage with antipseudomonal agents if healthcare-acquired pneumonia is suspected.
Switch from intravenous to oral antibiotics when patients are hemodynamically stable and clinically improving, are able to ingest medications, and have a normally functioning gastrointestinal tract.
Continue antibiotic therapy for at least 3 weeks or until radiologic resolution of abscess.
Consider surgical drainage if the patient is not responding to antibiotics, if an obstructing lesion is present, or if hemorrhage is present.
Percutaneous drainage is safe and effective for lung abscess and may be superior to conservative management.
A case report described use of endobronchial ultrasounography wih a guide sheath to successfully aspirate an abscess.
Postural drainage of the affected lobe is often recommended but clinical trials of efficacy are lacking.
Up to 35% mortality in pre-antibiotic era. C

Overall mortality is approximately 10% to 15%, but the mortality rate is higher in immunocompromized patients, those with preoperative sepsis or air leak, respiratory failure, or acute renal failure.B
In a series of 49 children with lung abscess (out of 5151 admitted with pneumonia). The CXR completely resolved in half of the children, and took a mean of 84 days.
Lung abscess can develop in edentulous persons as anaerobic bacteria can still be present in an edentulous oral cavity. Edentulous patients may also be prone to increased aspiration.
Rare in children; anaerobic infections are rarely seen in children younger than 6 years.
As in adults, fever, cough, and dyspnea are the most common presenting symptoms.
The treatment options are similar to those for adults; some medications, however, may not be recommended for children.
